subject: English
topic: Direct-indirect speech for questions — mixed tiers
description: Reporting Wh- and Yes/No questions; tense backshift, word order changes

questions.stem: Convert to indirect: 'He said to me, "Where do you live?"'

options.option_text: He asked me where I live now
He asked me where I lived then
He told me where I do live now
He asked me that where did I live

questions.explanation: Wh-question reporting: drop quotation, drop 'do/does/did', use straight word order, backshift tense. 'do live' → 'lived'. 'Asked' (not 'told' for questions). Distractor 1 — present tense, wrong. Distractor 3 — 'told' is for statements; 'do' should be dropped. Distractor 4 — 'that' is for statements; question structure (did) should not be retained.

questions.stem: Convert to indirect: 'She said to him, "Are you happy?"'

options.option_text: She asked him that he was happy
She asked him if he was happy
She told him are you happy now
She asked him whether is he happy

questions.explanation: Yes/No question reporting: use 'if' or 'whether', drop quotes, no 'that', backshift tense ('are' → 'was'), straight word order. Distractor 1 — 'that' wrongly used (it's for statements). Distractor 3 — 'told' for question is wrong; structure also broken. Distractor 4 — 'whether' OK but kept question inversion 'is he', wrong.

questions.stem: Convert to indirect: 'The teacher said, "Why are you late, Ravi?"'

options.option_text: The teacher told Ravi why was he late
The teacher asked Ravi why he was late
The teacher said Ravi why he is late
The teacher told Ravi if he was late then

questions.explanation: Wh-question to indirect: 'asked' (not 'told'), drop 'are' inversion ('was he' → 'he was'), retain wh-word, backshift tense. 'Are' → 'was'. Distractor 1 — kept inverted question form. Distractor 3 — 'said' should become 'asked' for questions; tense also wrong. Distractor 4 — 'if' is for yes/no questions, not wh-questions.

questions.stem: Convert to indirect: 'My brother said to me, "Did you complete the assignment?"'

options.option_text: My brother asked me did I complete it
My brother asked me if I had completed it
My brother told me whether I completed it
My brother asked me that I had completed it

questions.explanation: Yes/No past question: use 'if', drop 'did' inversion, backshift simple-past 'did complete' → past-perfect 'had completed'. Distractor 1 — kept 'did' inversion, wrong. Distractor 3 — 'told' is for statements. Distractor 4 — 'that' for statements; questions need 'if/whether'.

questions.stem: Convert to indirect: 'She said, "Will you help me with this?"'

options.option_text: She asked me would I help her with it
She asked me if I would help her with that
She said me whether I would help her with it
She told me that I would help her with it

questions.explanation: Yes/No future-modal question: 'will' → 'would' (backshift), use 'if', straight order, 'this' → 'that' for distance. Distractor 1 — kept 'would I' inversion. Distractor 3 — 'said me' is wrong (said + to me, OR asked me); also question needs 'asked'. Distractor 4 — 'told that' is for statements.

questions.stem: Convert to indirect: 'They said, "How long has she been waiting here?"'

options.option_text: They asked how long had she been waiting
They asked how long she had been waiting there
They said how long has she been waiting here
They told how long had she been waiting here

questions.explanation: Wh-question with present-perfect-continuous: 'has been' → 'had been' (backshift), drop inversion, 'here' → 'there'. Distractor 1 — kept 'had she' inversion. Distractor 3 — kept original tense + place adverb. Distractor 4 — 'told' for question + kept inversion.

questions.stem: Convert to indirect: 'The doctor said, "Have you eaten breakfast?"'

options.option_text: The doctor said have I eaten breakfast
The doctor asked if I had eaten breakfast
The doctor told me that I had eaten breakfast
The doctor asked whether had I eaten breakfast

questions.explanation: Yes/No present-perfect question: 'have eaten' → 'had eaten' (backshift), 'if' (or whether), drop inversion. Distractor 1 — kept question form + 'said'. Distractor 3 — 'told that' is for statements (loses question sense). Distractor 4 — kept 'had I' inversion.

questions.stem: Which option correctly converts to indirect speech: 'He asked his friend, "Where is the nearest hospital?"'?

options.option_text: He asked his friend where the nearest hospital is
He asked his friend where the nearest hospital was
He asked his friend where was the nearest hospital
He asked his friend that where the nearest hospital was

questions.explanation: B is correct because WH-questions convert to indirect speech by replacing question word order with statement order ('where the nearest hospital was') and backshifting present 'is' to past 'was'. Option A retains 'is' without backshift. Option C keeps interrogative word order ('where was the hospital'). Option D wrongly inserts 'that' before the WH-word, which is ungrammatical.

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect form of: 'Meena said to her sister, "Do you know the way to the post office?"'?

options.option_text: Meena asked her sister that she knew the way to the post office
Meena asked her sister that does she know the way to the post office
Meena asked her sister whether she knew the way to the post office
Meena asked her sister if she knows the way to the post office

questions.explanation: C is correct: yes/no questions use 'whether/if + statement word order + backshift'; 'Do you know' becomes 'whether she knew' ('said to' → 'asked', 'you' → 'she', 'know' → 'knew'). Options A and B wrongly use 'that', which introduces reported statements—not yes/no questions. Option D is the most tempting distractor but retains present tense 'knows' instead of backshifting to 'knew'.

questions.stem: Identify the correct indirect speech for: 'The officer said to the applicant, "Can you submit the documents by Friday?"'?

options.option_text: The officer asked the applicant if he could submit the documents by Friday
The officer asked the applicant that can he submit the documents by Friday
The officer asked the applicant whether he can submit the documents by Friday
The officer asked the applicant if could he submit the documents by Friday

questions.explanation: A is correct because the modal 'can' shifts to 'could' (backshift rule), and question word order inverts to statement order ('if he could submit'). Option B retains 'can' without backshift and uses ungrammatical 'that can he'. Option C also keeps 'can' without the required shift to 'could'. Option D inverts the subject-auxiliary wrongly ('if could he'), a common word-order trap in competitive exams.

questions.stem: Select the correct indirect form: 'She said to him, "Where did you go last evening?"'?

options.option_text: She asked him where had he gone the previous evening
She asked him where he went the previous evening
She asked him where he has gone the previous evening
She asked him where he had gone the previous evening

questions.explanation: D is correct: simple past 'did go' shifts to past perfect 'had gone', statement word order replaces question order, and 'last' shifts to 'the previous'. Option A retains interrogative word order ('where had he gone'). Option B uses simple past 'went' — the most common error, missing the obligatory shift to past perfect. Option C wrongly uses present perfect 'has gone', which moves in the wrong tense direction.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly reports: 'The inspector said to the constable, "Have you submitted the report yet?"'?

options.option_text: The inspector asked the constable that had he submitted the report yet
The inspector asked the constable whether he had submitted the report yet
The inspector asked the constable if he has submitted the report yet
The inspector asked the constable whether he submitted the report yet

questions.explanation: B is correct: present perfect 'have submitted' → past perfect 'had submitted' (backshift), yes/no question uses 'whether/if', statement word order, and 'yet' is retained unchanged. Option A uses 'that had he' — an ungrammatical blend of statement-introducer 'that' with question inversion. Option C keeps 'has submitted' with no backshift. Option D omits 'had', reducing past perfect to simple past 'submitted', which loses the aspect completely.

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect speech for: 'The manager said to the clerk, "Why haven't you replied to the client's email yet?"'?

options.option_text: The manager asked the clerk why he has not replied to the client's email yet
The manager asked the clerk why had he not replied to the client's email yet
The manager asked the clerk why he had not replied to the client's email yet
The manager asked the clerk that why he had not replied to the client's email

questions.explanation: C is correct: present perfect negative 'haven't replied' shifts to past perfect 'had not replied'; WH-word 'why' is retained and followed by statement word order ('he had not…'). Option A keeps 'has not replied' — failing the backshift of present perfect to past perfect, a very common error. Option B is tempting but retains question word order ('why had he not') instead of the required statement order. Option D uses 'that why', an ungrammatical double introducer.

questions.stem: Identify the correct indirect form: 'Rita said to her boss, "Am I supposed to submit two copies or one?"'?

options.option_text: Rita asked her boss if she is supposed to submit two copies or one
Rita asked her boss whether she was supposed to submit two copies or one
Rita asked her boss that was she supposed to submit two copies or one
Rita asked her boss whether was she supposed to submit two copies or one

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'or' questions offering two alternatives convert with 'whether…or' (not 'if…or'); 'Am I' shifts to 'she was' (pronoun 'I' → 'she', 'am' backshifts to 'was'). Option A uses 'if' (acceptable only for simple yes/no, not alternatives) and fails to backshift 'am' to 'was', keeping 'is'. Option C uses 'that was she' — a structural error blending statement-introducer 'that' with question inversion. Option D retains interrogative word order ('whether was she') — the classic trap even advanced students fall into.
